\sphinxlineitem{Calculate the reduced scatter (μs’) and absorption (μa) coefficients. See}
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{generated/photon_canon.contrib.bio:photon_canon.contrib.bio.inverse_power_law_for_reduced_scattering}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{inverse\_power\_law\_for\_reduced\_scattering()}}}}} and {\hyperref[\detokenize{generated/photon_canon.contrib.bio:photon_canon.contrib.bio.spectroscopic_model_of_absorption}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{spectroscopic\_model\_of\_absorption()}}}}} for
mathematical details. Coefficients are calculated from input parameters a, b, c and epsilon over the
wavelengths provided.

\end{description}

\pysigstartsignatures
\pysiglinewithargsret
{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{photon\_canon.contrib.bio.}}\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{hemoglobin\_mus}}}
{\sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{a}\DUrole{o}{=}\DUrole{default_value}{1}}\sphinxparamcomma \sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{b}\DUrole{o}{=}\DUrole{default_value}{1}}\sphinxparamcomma \sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{t}\DUrole{o}{=}\DUrole{default_value}{1}}\sphinxparamcomma \sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{s}\DUrole{o}{=}\DUrole{default_value}{0.5}}\sphinxparamcomma \sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{wavelengths}\DUrole{o}{=}\DUrole{default_value}{None}}\sphinxparamcomma \sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{force\_feasible}\DUrole{o}{=}\DUrole{default_value}{True}}}
{}
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
Computes the reduced scattering coefficient (μs’) for hemoglobin solutions
based on given absorption coefficients of oxyhemoglobin (HbO2) and deoxyhemoglobin (Hb). See {\hyperref[\detokenize{generated/photon_canon.contrib.bio:photon_canon.contrib.bio.calculate_mus}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{calculate\_mus()}}}}}
for more details.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Default values are supplied via Scott Prahl at \sphinxurl{https://omlc.org/spectra/hemoglobin/summary.html}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function interpolates the extinction coefficients of HbO2 and Hb
at specified wavelengths using cubic interpolation and calculates the
corresponding μs’ values.
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{force\_feasible}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{bool}}) \textendash{} Option to prevent impossible values (like negative concentrations) (default: True)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{a}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{Real}}) \textendash{} Scattering amplitude for the reduced scattering coefficient (default: 1).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{b}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{Real}}) \textendash{} Scattering power exponent (default: 1).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{t}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{Real}}) \textendash{} Total hemoglobin concentration (tHb) in g/L (default: \sphinxtitleref{tHb}).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{s}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{Real}}) \textendash{} Oxygen saturation (sO2) as a fraction (0 to 1) (default: \sphinxtitleref{sO2}).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{wavelengths}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{Iterable}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{{[}}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{Real}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{{]}}}) \textendash{} Array of wavelengths (in nm) at which to compute the values (default: \sphinxtitleref{wl}).

\end{itemize}

\sphinxlineitem{Returns}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A tuple containing:
\sphinxhyphen{} The reduced scattering coefficient (μs’) at each wavelength.
\sphinxhyphen{} The interpolated extinction coefficient for THb.
\sphinxhyphen{} The wavelengths of the measures (passed unchanged from input, useful for defaulting and reusing)

\sphinxlineitem{Return type}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Tuple{[}Real, Real, Real{]} or Tuple{[}NDArray, NDArray, NDArray{]}

\sphinxlineitem{Notes}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The extinction coefficients for HbO2 and Hb are interpolated using cubic
interpolation from a predefined dataset.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Extrapolation is used for wavelengths outside the dataset range.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The calculation assumes a power\sphinxhyphen{}law dependence on wavelength for scattering.

\end{itemize}

\end{description}\end{quote}

\end{fulllineitems}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

Forwarding function to streamline \(\mathrm{[tHb]\,\&\,\mathrm{sO_2}\) modelling. This function takes biological parameters and turns them
optical properties, then forwards those to model reflectance and returns that reflectance. In short, biological
properties get converted to reflectance using the given model. See {\hyperref[\detokenize{generated/photon_canon.contrib.bio:photon_canon.contrib.bio.hemoglobin_mus}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{hemoglobin\_mus()}}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{generated/photon_canon.contrib.bio:photon_canon.contrib.bio.calculate_mus}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{calculate\_mus()}}}}} for more details.

{}
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
Build a callable that returns the \sphinxstylestrong{radially integrated diffuse
reflectance}
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\tilde{R}_d(\mu_s, \mu_a)
\;=\;
2\pi \int_{r_{\min}}^{r_{\max}}
r \, R_d\!\bigl(r;\mu_s,\mu_a\bigr)\;dr,\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(R_d(r;\mu_s,\mu_a)\) is the spatially resolved
reflectance given by {\hyperref[\detokenize{generated/photon_canon.contrib.diffusion_theory:photon_canon.contrib.diffusion_theory.diffusion_approximation}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{diffusion\_approximation()}}}}}.


\subsubsection{Parameters}
\label{\detokenize{generated/photon_canon.contrib.diffusion_theory:parameters}}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{r\_range}{[}(float, float){]}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Integration bounds \((r_{\min}, r_{\max})\) in millimetres.

\sphinxlineitem{alpha\_i}{[}float, optional{]}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Angle of incidence of the illumination in \sphinxstylestrong{radians}
(\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{0}} ⇒ normal incidence). Default \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{0}}.

\sphinxlineitem{n\_rel}{[}float, optional{]}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Relative refractive index \(n_2/n_1\)
(tissue / external medium). Default \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{1.33}}.

\sphinxlineitem{g}{[}float, optional{]}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Scattering anisotropy factor. Default \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{0.9}}.

\end{description}


\subsubsection{Returns}
\label{\detokenize{generated/photon_canon.contrib.diffusion_theory:returns}}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Callable{[}{[}float, float{]}, float{]}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A function \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{f(mu\_s, mu\_a)}} that evaluates
\(\tilde{R}_d(\mu_s,\mu_a)\) using
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{scipy.integrate.quad()}}.

\end{description}


\subsubsection{Notes}
\label{\detokenize{generated/photon_canon.contrib.diffusion_theory:notes}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The integrand is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}f(r,\mu_s,\mu_a)
\;=\;
2\pi\,r\,R_d(r;\mu_s,\mu_a),\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
so the returned function effectively computes
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\tilde{R}_d(\mu_s,\mu_a)
\;=\;
\int_{r_{\min}}^{r_{\max}} f(r,\mu_s,\mu_a)\;dr.\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The numerical integration is performed with adaptive quadrature
(\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{scipy.integrate.quad()}}).

\subsubsection{Notes}
\label{\detokenize{generated/photon_canon.contrib.diffusion_theory:id1}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The diffusion approximation is valid when
\(\mu_s' \gg \mu_a\), where the \sphinxstylestrong{reduced scattering
coefficient} is \(\mu_s' = (1-g)\,\mu_s\).
Key intermediate quantities are
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mu_t' &= \mu_s' + \mu_a \\
l'     &= \frac{1}{\mu_t'} \\
a'     &= \frac{\mu_s'}{\mu_t'} \\[6pt]
D      &= \frac{1}{3\left(\mu_s' + \beta\mu_a\right)}, \qquad
         \beta = \begin{cases}
           1 & \text{normal incidence} \\
           0.35 & \text{oblique incidence}
         \end{cases} \\[6pt]
\mu_{\mathrm{eff}} &= \sqrt{\frac{\mu_a}{D}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The diffuse reflectance is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}R_d(r) \;=\; \bigl(1-R_{\mathrm{sp}}\bigr)
\Bigl[
    a' z' \,
    \frac{\bigl(1+\mu_{\mathrm{eff}}\rho_1\bigr)
          e^{-\mu_{\mathrm{eff}}\rho_1}}{4\pi\rho_1^{3}}
    \;+\;
    a'\!\bigl(z' + 4D\bigr)
    \frac{\bigl(1+\mu_{\mathrm{eff}}\rho_2\bigr)
          e^{-\mu_{\mathrm{eff}}\rho_2}}{4\pi\rho_2^{3}}
\Bigr],\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\rho_1\) and \(\rho_2\) are the distances from the
observation point to the real and image sources, respectively, and
\(R_{\mathrm{sp}}\) is the specular Fresnel reflectance.

\subsubsection{Notes}
\label{\detokenize{generated/photon_canon.contrib.food_coloring:notes}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The mixture obeys the Beer\textendash{}Lambert law, so absorbances \sphinxstylestrong{add
linearly}:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}A(\lambda) \;=\;
\sum_{i} c_i\,a_i(\lambda),\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(a_i(\lambda)\) is the \sphinxstyleemphasis{per\sphinxhyphen{}unit} absorbance spectrum of dye
\sphinxstyleemphasis{i} (1 µL / mL reference), and

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(c_i\) is the requested concentration (µL/mL).

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The premixed stocks are treated exactly the same way, using their
own per\sphinxhyphen{}unit spectra.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Bases: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{BaseModel}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Lookup table class that acts as an interface to generated LUT data. This class includes callability with one or
multiple parameters, with the parameter call order set at LUT object creation by \sphinxtitleref{dimensions}. When called, the LUT
will automatically handle extrapolation based on its settings and return the response value accordingly. The LUT
surface can be smoothed by passing a smoohting\_fn, which is applied to the grid at interpolation time. The LUT also
provides several methods to visualize or access the underlying LUT data. Finally, class/instance methods of the LUT
class provide a simplified interface for querying the available information across multiple simulations.
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{simulation\_id}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{int}}) \textendash{} The ID of the generated LUT to access.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{dimensions}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{List}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{{[}}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{str}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{{]}}}) \textendash{} The dimensions to consider at lookup in the LUT. The order will be used for calls. Default: ‘mu\_s’, ‘mu\_a’, ‘g’.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{extrapolate}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{bool}}) \textendash{} Whether to extrapolate outside the table bounds. Overrideable at call time as a kwarg. Default: False.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{scale}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{float}}) \textendash{} The scale to compare responses against to normalize (if needed). Default: 1.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{smoothing\_fn}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{callable}}) \textendash{} A function that will be applied to the response grid. Optional. Default: None.

\end{itemize}

\end{description}\end{quote}

Get the surface information for the LUT. Returns all unique values of each of the first 2 dimensions and the grid of responses at those dimensions. This allows for quick and easy visualization using ax.plot\_wireframe(X, Y, Z). Note, this surface will include smoothing if self.smoothing\_fn is not None.

Simulates photon transport for different optical properties to generate a lookup table (LUT).

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function iterates over the input arrays, modifying the optical properties of \sphinxtitleref{variable}
(a \sphinxtitleref{Medium} object) accordingly. A set of \sphinxtitleref{Photon} objects is then simulated within the \sphinxtitleref{system}.

Simple tally detector that counts photons accepted by a user\sphinxhyphen{}supplied
\sphinxstylestrong{acceptance function}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The detector maintains two running counters:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{n\_total}}    \textendash{} total weight of photons presented.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{n\_detected}} \textendash{} weight of photons whose exit positions and
directions satisfy the acceptance criterion.

\end{itemize}
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{acceptor}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{Callable}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{{[}}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{{[}}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{numpy.ndarray}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{, }}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{numpy.ndarray}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{{]}}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{, }}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{numpy.ndarray}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{{]}}}) \textendash{} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Callable that decides if a photon hits the detector.
It is called as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{acceptor(x, y, mu\_z=mu\_z)}} where
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{x, y}} \textendash{} exit coordinates of each photon (mm),

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mu\_z}}  \textendash{} := \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cos(θ\_exit)}} (z\sphinxhyphen{}component of direction).

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Must return a Boolean array of the same length.
The default is an aperture defined by
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{create\_cone\_of\_acceptance()}}.


\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{desc}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{str}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{ | }}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{None}}) \textendash{} Optional description string.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxlineitem{Variables}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{n\_total}} \textendash{} Cumulative \sphinxstyleemphasis{weight} of all photons processed.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{n\_detected}} \textendash{} Cumulative \sphinxstyleemphasis{weight} of photons accepted.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{acceptor}} \textendash{} Acceptance function provided at construction.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{description}} \textendash{} Raw description string.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxlineitem{Raises}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{ValueError}} \textendash{} If \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\_\_call\_\_()}} is invoked with an object
that is not a {\hyperref[\detokenize{generated/photon_canon.optics:photon_canon.optics.Photon}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Photon}}}}}.

\end{description}\end{quote}

\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{The object tracks each photon’s wavelength, position, direction and statistical weight while it propagates through}
\sphinxAtStartPar
an optical {\hyperref[\detokenize{generated/photon_canon.optics:photon_canon.optics.System}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{System}}}}}. Built\sphinxhyphen{}in routines handle movement, scattering, absorption,
interface interactions and Russian\sphinxhyphen{}roulette termination.

\end{description}

Decrements the weights of the photon batch according to the albedo of the current medium.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This method simulates the absorption of photons in the current medium. The weights of each photon is
reduced based on the albedo, which represents the fraction of light that is reflected. The remaining
weights is used to continue the photon simulation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The specific absorption process depends on the optical properties of the medium the photon is currently in.

\index{move() (photon\_canon.optics.Photon method)@\spxentry{move()}\spxextra{photon\_canon.optics.Photon method}}

\begin{fulllineitems}

{\sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{step}\DUrole{o}{=}\DUrole{default_value}{None}}}
{}
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
Moves the photon one step in its current direction.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The size of the step can be either provided directly, or it can be determined by the mean free path of the
current medium, which is calculated from the transport coefficient (mu\_t). If the photon is in a medium with
mu\_t = 0 (i.e., no scattering or absorption), the photon will automatically advance to the next interface along
its direction.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If a step size is provided, the photon moves in the direction specified by its directional cosines until it
either completes the step or hits an interface. If the full step would cross an interface, only the portion of
the step before the interface is executed. At the interface, the photon is refracted and reflected according to
the media properties, and its weights is updated (decremented) based on the interaction.
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{step}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{float}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{ | }}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{Iterable}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{{[}}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{float}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{{]}}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{, }}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{optional}}) \textendash{} The distance the photon should move. If not provided, the step size is sampled based on the mean
free path, \(-\frac{\ln\xi}{\mu_t}\)

\sphinxlineitem{Raises}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{ValueError}} \textendash{} If \sphinxstyleemphasis{step} is an array of incompatible shape.

\sphinxlineitem{Return type}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{sphinx_autodoc_typehints-type}{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{None}}}

\sphinxlineitem{Returns}
\sphinxAtStartPar
None. The photon’s location coordinates and directions are updated.

\end{description}\end{quote}

\end{fulllineitems}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Computes photon reflection and refraction at interfaces.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This method determines the weight of photon reflection and updates the tracker’s direction accordingly.
If reflection occurs, it either updates the photon direction or spawns secondary photons with adjusted weights
to continue the recursive simulation. The photon’s direction is updated based on the interface’s refractive
values. This operation is performed only on photons specified by the input mask.

\item {}

is present.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Simulates the behavior of a batch of photons until all photons are terminated and updates the object’s
attributes accordingly.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The simulation involves the following steps:
\sphinxhyphen{} \sphinxstylestrong{Absorption}: Photons interact with the medium and may be absorbed. (See \sphinxtitleref{self.absorb}).
\sphinxhyphen{} \sphinxstylestrong{Movement}: Photons move within the medium. (See \sphinxtitleref{self.move}).
\sphinxhyphen{} \sphinxstylestrong{Scattering}: Photons may scatter as they travel through the medium. (See \sphinxtitleref{self.scatter}).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The exact behavior of these events depends on the optical properties of the \sphinxtitleref{Medium} object the photon is in,
which is determined through queries to the \sphinxtitleref{System} that contains the photon, i.e., \sphinxtitleref{self.system}.
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Returns}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This method runs the simulation and does not return any value.

\sphinxlineitem{Return type}
\sphinxAtStartPar
None

\end{description}\end{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar
Determines the first interfaces crossed when moving between two locations, considering only the z\sphinxhyphen{}coordinates.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This method checks if any interfaces boundaries lie between the given z\sphinxhyphen{}coordinates. If an interfaces is crossed,
the method calculates its z\sphinxhyphen{}location and identifies the two mediums forming the interfaces.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\#\#\# Process:
1. Identify boundaries that fall between the start and end z\sphinxhyphen{}coordinates.
2. Compute the distance from the start z\sphinxhyphen{}coordinate to each boundary.
3. Apply a mask to filter boundaries that are actually crossed.
4. Select the closest crossed boundary as the interfaces plane.
5. Determine the two mediums making up the interfaces by slightly shifting the plane’s z\sphinxhyphen{}coordinate:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Backwards (toward the start) to find the first medium.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Forwards (away from the start) to find the second medium.

\end{itemize}
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{location1}} (\DUrole{sphinx_autodoc_typehints-type}{Iterable{[}float{]}}) \textendash{} Starting location of the query.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{location2}} \textendash{} Ending location of the query.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxlineitem{Return type}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\DUrole{sphinx_autodoc_typehints-type}{Tuple{[}Medium | (), float | None{]}}

\sphinxlineitem{Returns}
\sphinxAtStartPar

plane at which the interface is crossed or None.

Generalizes reflectance modeling by applying a provided model function to arrays of scattering and absorption coefficients.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function computes modeled reflectance based on the given \sphinxtitleref{model}, scattering coefficients (\sphinxtitleref{mu\_s}),
and absorption coefficients (\sphinxtitleref{mu\_a}). If \sphinxtitleref{vectorize} is set to True, the function assumes that the model
supports vectorized input and calls it once for all values. Otherwise, it loops through each pair
of (\sphinxtitleref{mu\_s}, \sphinxtitleref{mu\_a}) values and computes the reflectance individually.
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{model}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{Callable}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{{[}}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{{[}}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{float}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{, }}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{float}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{, }}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{...}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{{]}}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{, }}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{Union}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{{[}}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{float}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{, }}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{np.ndarray}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{{]}}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{{]}}}) \textendash{} A function that accepts \sphinxtitleref{mu\_s}, \sphinxtitleref{mu\_a}, and optional keyword arguments to return reflectance.
Must return either a float or a NumPy array.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{mu\_s}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{np.ndarray}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{{[}}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{float}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{{]}}}) \textendash{} An array of scattering coefficients, μs.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{mu\_a}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{np.ndarray}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{{[}}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{float}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{{]}}}) \textendash{} An array of absorption coefficients, μa.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{vectorize}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{bool}}) \textendash{} Whether to evaluate the model in a vectorized fashion. If False, uses a loop.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{kwargs}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{Any}}) \textendash{} Additional keyword arguments to pass to the model function.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxlineitem{Returns}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Array of modeled reflectance values corresponding to each (\sphinxtitleref{mu\_s}, \sphinxtitleref{mu\_a}) pair.

\sphinxlineitem{Return type}
\sphinxAtStartPar
np.ndarray{[}float{]}

\end{description}\end{quote}

\end{fulllineitems}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Samples a wavelength from a spectral probability distribution.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The function normalizes the input spectrum to form a probability density function (PDF),
computes the cumulative distribution function (CDF), and uses inverse transform sampling
to randomly select a wavelength based on the distribution.

\chapter{Photon Canon}
\label{\detokenize{README:photon-canon}}\label{\detokenize{README::doc}}\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A python toolbox for in\sphinxhyphen{}depth 3D Monte Carlo simulation with custom systems of planar mediums, custom beams and
detectors
\end{quote}

\section{Project Description}
\label{\detokenize{README:project-description}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Photon\sphinxhyphen{}canon is a fully parallel Monte Carlo simulation framework with support for custom optical systems and devices.
Users can create custom optical \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Medium}} objects with wavelength\sphinxhyphen{}dependent attributes, stack these into planar \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{System}}
objects, and simulate \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Photon}} objects within their system. The injection of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Photon}} objects can be controlled through
user\sphinxhyphen{}defined custom \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Illumination}} objects that define direction and location of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Photon}} initialization, with simple
compatibility with user\sphinxhyphen{}defined samplers. Additionally, custom \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Detector}} objects provide spatial resolution for
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Photon}} exit locations, to provide precise forward\sphinxhyphen{}problem modelling that can decrease loss in inverse fitting.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{System}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Photon}} objects also include plot features to allow for qualitatively troubleshooting and checks for
expected behaviors. These also are just fun to look at.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxincludegraphics{{simulation}.png}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Try it for yourself.} Submit a \sphinxhref{https://www.github.com/jiversivers/photon\_canon/issues/new/choose}{Simulate Me!}
issue to update the sample simulation shown here with your own parameters.


\subsection{Different builds}
\label{\detokenize{README:different-builds}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The default build (with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cupy}}) provides vectorized GPU\sphinxhyphen{}compatibility for rapid, parallel generation of simulation\sphinxhyphen{}based
lookup tables. When run on the CPU, the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{numpy}} build still provides an at least order of magnitudes speed up over
equivalent one\sphinxhyphen{}by\sphinxhyphen{}one simulations. When installing on a system without a CUDA\sphinxhyphen{}compatible GPU, the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{numpy}} build must be
used. See {\hyperref[\detokenize{README:install-with-pip}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{xref}{\DUrole{myst}{installation}}}}} for more details.

\subsection{Photon}
\label{\detokenize{README:photon}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Photon}} object type is the real work\sphinxhyphen{}horse of the simulation. The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Photon}} object is a bit of a misnomer, as it
should actually be thought of as a packet of photons. By allowing the object to actually hold many thousands of photon,
simulations can be parallelized to greatly increase the speed. A \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Photon}} object may have any \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{batch\_size}} that a
systems memory can handle, but is single in its wavelength and system, however. The output attributes, T, R, and A are
trackers of all \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{batch\_size}} members. When considering the appropriate \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{batch\_size}}, many factors come into play. A
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Photon}} object will occupy a space on memory depending on the number of steps of a simulation, which is dependent on
the properties of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{System}}. Generally, a low\sphinxhyphen{}absorbing, high\sphinxhyphen{}scattering system will have long simulations, so
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{batch\_size}} should be smaller. High\sphinxhyphen{}abosrbing, low\sphinxhyphen{}scattering systems will simulate in very few steps, and can handle
higher \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{batch\_size}} inputs. Consider that the location coordinates for a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{batch\_size}} of 50,000 occupy \textasciitilde{}1.2 GB of
memory. As the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Photon}} is simulated, its space in RAM only increases as trackers of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{weight}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{location}} augment.
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Photon}} object is responsible for tracking and updating the information of the simulation, including all photon
locations, directions, current mediums, weights, etc. It is fully vectorized and supports recursing photons, that are
created at index\sphinxhyphen{}mismatched interface reflections. The precision with which this framework was designed, does open the
door for very long\sphinxhyphen{}lived photons, either through deep recursion (though this is unlikely), or through total internal
reflection (this is much more probable). Options are included to limit these behaviors, though it is recommended that
they are left on initially, and only switched off or limited if necessary. In most cases, these behaviors have minimal
effect in simulation time, but have slight impacts on simulation outputs. Members of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Photon}} objects can be simulated
until they are terminated, which occurs when they either exit their \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{System}} or have a weight of 0. Once they are
terminated, their location and direction will not change, but the full object simulation may continue until all members
are terminated, at which point, querying \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{photon.is\_terminated}} returns \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{True}}, and additional simulation steps will
have no effect (though \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{move()}} method calls will extend the location history trivially). \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Photon}} objects include
attributes, T, R, and A, to track cummulative outcomes of members. They can be simulated manually and step\sphinxhyphen{}wise using
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{absorb()}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{move()}}, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{scatter()}} methods, or using the builtin \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{simulate()}} method which runs until all members are
terminated.

\subsubsection{Medium}
\label{\detokenize{README:medium}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Medium}} objects are simply wrappers for optical properties, namely, n, μs, μa, and g.
These properties can either be defined as scalars for the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{medium}} or as a wavelength\sphinxhyphen{}dependent arrays that can then be
interpolated used to determine their value at an input wavelength. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Photon}} objects query the medium to determine the
necessary properties of their current medium at any point. The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Photon}} only ‘knows’ the properties of the location it
in, nothing else. The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Medium}} object, when stacked into a system, gives the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Photon}} this information.


\subsubsection{System}
\label{\detokenize{README:system}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{System}} objects are the connection between \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Medium}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Photon}} objects. A \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{System}} is made up of one or more \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Medium}}
objects stacked with specified thicknesses from 0 cm and on. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{System}} objects can be finite or semi\sphinxhyphen{}infinite. Finite
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{System}} objects are filled on both the negative and positive infinity sides with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{surroundings}}. When semi\sphinxhyphen{}infinite,
they will be filled with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{surroundings}} only on the negative infinity side. The n of surroundings can be manually
defined in the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{System}}, as this value controls the reflection intensity of exiting \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Photon}} objects. For most
light\sphinxhyphen{}matter interactions that this framework simulates, the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Photon}} object uses the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{System}} as a mediator to query
the optical properties of the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Medium}}, as the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{System}} holds the spatial information necessary to determine the current
medium, given a location. The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{System}} is also key in detemrming the completion of simulation, as a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Photon}} is
terminated when it exits the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{System}}.


\subsection{Illuminator}
\label{\detokenize{README:illuminator}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Illumination}} objects are simply sampler wrappers. They provide an easy API to automate the sampling of illumination
photons from user defined functions. When added to a system, they can be used to obtain spatially distributed \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Photon}}
objects. They are always placed into systems centered at the (0, 0, 0). transparent media can be stacked beneath this to
effectively change the starting point.


\subsection{Detector}
\label{\detokenize{README:detector}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Similar to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Illuminator}} objects, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Detector}} objects are wrappers for user defined functions. These are boolean\sphinxhyphen{}based
and return whether a location and, optionally, direction would be detected. The object automatically counts how the
weight queried and the weight detected. If not weight is input when the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Detector}} is queried, then it is assumed to be
unity. At any time, counts can be reset with the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{reset()}} method. This is useful to allow the same object to be used
in iterative simulations, such as when creating a lookup table.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Unlike \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Illuminator}} objects, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Detector}} objects must include a z coordinate when stacked into a system. They will be
centered at (0, 0, z). The user\sphinxhyphen{}defined detection pattern can be used to offset the detection in the x and y directions.
By using multiple detector objects with different offsets, a detector array can be created to spatially resolve photon
detection even further.

\section{Installation}
\label{\detokenize{README:installation}}

\subsection{Basic Install}
\label{\detokenize{README:basic-install}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To install the project and its dependencies, run the following command:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
pip\PYG{+w}{ }install\PYG{+w}{ }photon\PYGZhy{}canon
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{\sphinxstyleemphasis{NOTE:}} By default, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pip}} will not install \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cupy}}. On systems without a CUDA\sphinxhyphen{}GPU, this is the desired behavior,
but you will receive an import warning when using this package. IF you have a compatible GPU, see below for CUDA
options.
\end{quote}


\subsection{CUDA Systems}
\label{\detokenize{README:cuda-systems}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you have a compatible GPU, you can run \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{photon\sphinxhyphen{}canon}} with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cupy}} asa drop\sphinxhyphen{}in for numpy. If you already have cupy
installed, this will be the default behavior. If not, you can install it with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{photon\sphinxhyphen{}canon}} by calling the optional
dependencies for CUDA as follows:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
pip\PYG{+w}{ }install\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}photon\PYGZhy{}canon[cuda]\PYGZdq{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}
